blocks.2: The youth society Vårbrud, forerunner of Eivindvik youth society, founded in 1898. Picture of the first members, probably taken in 1899 outside N.G.A. Dahl's Herresalen. Photo: Unknown
blocks.3: Everyday life in Eivindvik has probably been much as in other villages in our parts. People toiled at their work, but they also took time off, relaxed at festive gatherings, visited each other and surely had a lot of home-made fun and many pleasant times in the homes around the village. When societies and organisations came, larger gatherings, such as meetings and parties, were arranged through them. Reading the youth society's paper gives a good picture of how people lived. At first the paper was called “Fremad” (Forward); later the name became “Opp og Fram” (Up and Onward), the same as the words on the society's banner.
blocks.4: People complained about bad weather with lots of rain, about drought and cold, then as now. The paper of 29 December 1927, for example, says in “Village news”: “If the drought and frost continue, we here in the village may soon have to fetch water from Dingja instead of electricity”. At Dingja they had then already had electric power for over 10 years. The Dinge river was developed from 1911 to 1917 by Johannes Steine, who used the power for his barrel factory.
blocks.5: One year there was so little snow that they could not go skiing in Midtundalen, but the trip was saved when snow came at Easter. 1928 was a record year as far as the weather went, because there was unusually heavy rain, especially in the summer months, and not least because there were 8 bridal couples in the village that year; “most married for the first time, but one set a rare record by marrying for the fourth time”. This is in the paper for 26 December 1928. In those days divorce was rare, so this must have been someone who had already been widowed 3 times.
blocks.6: The opposite of 1928 must have been 1904. On 8 January 1905 the paper reports, in a look back at the past year, that little happened in Midtunvågen – no engagements and so no weddings – so the priest and the parish clerk will soon forget “how a wedding is to be performed”. The author of the piece thinks the girls in a previous leap year were “far too quiet”, and they would surely come to regret it, for “soon all the brave lads will go out and fight the Swedes, and then only widowers will be left here, and they are few.”
blocks.7: From the start and on into the first part of our century, the content of the paper clearly shows that people were influenced by “the authorities”. The inherited respect, especially for the priest, surely lingered. Much of the material was what one must call educational, with many instructive and very good pieces, but there are also many examples of good folk humour. An example from the issue of 17 December 1899: “The Mormon and the farmer.”
blocks.8: Are you baptised? Yes. Do you remember it? No. Then you are not baptised.
blocks.9: May I ask a couple of questions too? Please do.
blocks.10: Were you born? Yes. Do you remember it? No. Then you were not born, you must be a ghost – out with you!
blocks.11: 21 January 1900: “One offends women by looking at them too much; one hurts them by not looking at them enough”.
blocks.12: In the same issue I see landsmål (Nynorsk) used in a story for the first time: a boy summoned to the district judge was asked to sit down, but despite the judge's repeated urging he remained standing, because there were no more chairs than for the judge and the clerk. When the judge shouted, “Sit down, I say!” the boy said: “No, it's like in Father's cowshed at home.” “How is it there, then?” “Well, there aren't more stalls than there are cattle.”
blocks.13: At the society's meetings there were often readings and debates on a subject, introduced by someone who knew about it. Taking part in the entertainment, and perhaps especially the debates, helped people loosen up so that they found the courage to stand up and speak when needed.
blocks.14: There was a lot of singing, in the church, in the youth society and elsewhere in the village, which promoted well-being and created a good culture. The many good pieces and fine home-made poems in the paper show that over the years there have been many fine talents in the village. Altogether the work of the societies and associations showed that there were many good, unnamed creators of culture in the countryside.
blocks.15: In the youth society, tree planting was an important cause early on. The minutes of an inspection at the parsonage on 15 August 1908 mention that about 70 decares of the farm's outlying land is “enclosed and planted with various kinds of trees” and that it is “Midtunvågen youth society” that “has done most of the planting work”. (The society was called “Vårbrudd”, so this is written wrongly in the minutes.) At Midtun, too, they became involved in tree planting early on, and in “Fremad” for 30 December 1911 I have found a poem about “Midttunskogen” (the Midtun forest). It is signed H.V. (Hans Vatne? He spent a good deal of time in Midtunvågen, and I know he wrote several poems), and goes like this:
blocks.16: “The Midttun farms lie cultivated and level,
blocks.17: the farmers there can eat their fill
blocks.18: and go to their work so glad and secure.
blocks.19: To the south there is nothing to shut out the sun;
blocks.20: if the north wind comes with cold from the pole,
blocks.21: they have the pine forest at their backs.
blocks.22: From pine and spruce tops the birds sing!
blocks.23: That is something other than heather.
blocks.24: You wanderer who comes along the path
blocks.26: I advise you: there are important things!
blocks.27: Should you lose your way in the forest,
blocks.28: you will learn, so sadly late,
blocks.29: that it was better to go round the forest.
blocks.30: The little birds flit and dart in there
blocks.31: in the forest that stands dense.
blocks.32: When you come in along the Midttun road
blocks.33: and the sun shines over the whole lot,
blocks.34: what is the most beautiful thing you get to see?
blocks.35: Is it the houses and the infield with drained bogs,
blocks.36: Joan's potatoes that are not weeded?
blocks.37: No, is it not the hillside planted with trees,
blocks.38: the lushest forest in all our hamlet
blocks.40: Yes, it can show what people can do
blocks.41: when they meet in earnest and take counsel together
blocks.42: and show in deeds that there is something they want.
blocks.43: And we who want to clothe our homeland with forest,
blocks.44: we know, yes we see, that our Lord with joy
blocks.45: so richly gives his blessing to it.
blocks.46: The farmer who does not hold the forest cause dear –
blocks.48: The first years of this century were tense times in our country; the society's paper mentions a possible war with the Swedes, and the government is criticised. Here is a little from a poem of 29 January 1905:
blocks.49: That statesmen's breasts are so lavishly decorated
blocks.51: because they have governed our country so well –
blocks.52: I do not think that is needed.”
blocks.53: On 8 January 1905 there is a poem about thoughts at the turn of the year, and the last verse goes like this:
blocks.56: set Him as rudder and anchor,
blocks.60: then we shall find the way
blocks.62: There have also been contributions on women and the vote, as this verse from 4 December 1904 recalls:
blocks.64: if we got an old woman as chief
blocks.66: Yes, one would see one's country advanced
blocks.67: if she were kept at home
blocks.68: to look after house and food.”
blocks.69: This would hardly have been written so today, with a prime minister called Gro, who is actually quite good.
blocks.70: I would like to include a couple of sayings from 10 April 1910:
blocks.71: “Life is not meant to be a torment for many and a feast for some, but for all a task that everyone must render account for.”
blocks.72: “It is poor fare to eat one's own words.”
blocks.73: “If every lie knocked out a tooth, there would be many toothless people.”
blocks.74: And then some glimpses from a report of the parish priest Ottesen's speech to the continuation school pupils, “and some guests”, at a party on 25 February 1911:
blocks.75: “People are never finished in life; they must develop at all times.”
blocks.76: “Culture is the same as cultivation, preferably cultivation of the soil. Farming is the best cultural work there is in the world.”
blocks.77: “..all honest and conscientious work according to God's will is fine and bears culture.”
blocks.78: The “Own hall” association worked as a “sub-department” of the youth society. Here the girls met, and with knitting, embroidery, sewing and so on they made masses of fine things that they raffled at bazaars to raise money for the society's own meeting hall. They did a great deal of work here.
blocks.81: The parsonage association in the 1920s. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.82: In the picture we see: front row from the left: Wilhelmine Hanssen, Sygni Tveit, Solveig Midthun, Olina Hauge, Gjertrud Underthun and Elisa Takle. 2nd row: Kristine Henriksbø, Gjertrud Sandal, Marta Myren (in Urda), Margrete Midthun, the parish priest Olaf Ottesen, Anna Undertun, Orlaug Korsvold and Andrine Henriksbø. 3rd row: Janna J. Sætre (Fagerbakken), Marie Henriksbø, Julia Fosse, Jørna Midthun, Serine Johannesdotter (Storesørina), Anna Hjellestad, Tilla Fosse, Ølla Navdal and Hansine Ellingsen. Back row: Anna Norstein, Marie Skauge, Guri Færevik, Anna Undal and Ragna Tveit (the parish clerk's wife).
blocks.83: There were also other associations in the village, for example mission associations such as the Seamen's Mission and the Norwegian Missionary Society. Later came the health association and the support association for the rescue boats.
blocks.84: The most important mission association was probably that of the Norwegian Missionary Society, which was called “the parsonage association” because the meetings were held at the parsonage, and it was the priests' wives who ran the association. Most of the women in the village gathered here for regular meetings. There is a picture from one such meeting where 28 people are present, and it has been possible to find the names of everyone in the picture. The picture was probably taken around the mid-1920s. The parish priest Ottesen is in it, and he left here in 1927. This association was alive until quite recently.
blocks.85: Our village got a choir early on. At a choir party at Undertun, Otto L. Midthun received a gift and much praise for his work with singing and leading the singing in the village. He started with the children, but gradually the adults joined in too, first the women. Later it was largely the teachers who took care of the choir. On 21 January 1900 the youth society's paper urged people to join “the singing society”, and the paper of 28 October the same year says that interest in singing has become great; the boys have joined too. Over the years the choir has given much good entertainment and been a source of great joy, both for audiences and for the singers themselves.
blocks.86: The village also had “the Gula rifle club”, “the Gula sports club” and “the Gula temperance society”. In “Fremad” for 29 January 1905 the idea was floated that “Vaarbrudd”, “the Gula rifle club” and “the Gula sports club” should build a hall of their own. The rifle club was founded as early as 1878 and has produced many good marksmen who have made the club known and brought fine challenge trophies to the village. The club has built up a good shooting range and has earned a very good reputation as an able organiser of competitions. Shooting is the sport that attracted the most interest here until football became so popular. Most men in the village were members of the rifle club, some girls too, and there was a very good team spirit and fellowship. There were many pleasant times at the shooting range, both at work and at competitions.
blocks.87: “The Gula sports club” has become Eivindvik sports club.
blocks.88: About “the Gula temperance society”, “Fremad” of 21 January 1906 has a report of a very successful party the society held at the consecration of its banner on 14 January 1906. The hall was beautifully decorated, and there was a lot of good entertainment. It was the teacher Hanssen (father of the Kristian Hanssen mentioned earlier) and Mrs Nilsen who had arranged the party (with many helpers). Mrs Ottesen was responsible for decorating the hall and “the cooking and laying of the tables”, with help from Mrs Hanssen, Rikka Risnes and Brita Ødegård. Hanssen opened the gathering, gave the unveiling speech and read poems. Mrs Nilsen also gave a speech “on community feeling”, and “Mrs Ottesen and her daughter” played the piano; among other things Mrs Ottesen played “the march to Haakon VII”. She also gave a reading, and “Mr J. Henriksbø recited a splendid poem about the temperance cause. He is quite a master at such things”. Jakob Pedersen Haukøy closed with a prayer. The stand-in priest, Arstein, also gave a speech “in his home dialect, and easily and freely.” “If only he would speak like that in church too”.
blocks.89: J. Henriksbø is the man we called Jo i Brekka. He was very good at reciting poems and was much in demand for it. Among other things he was greatly praised for his performances of “Terje Vigen”. Jakob Pedersen Haukøy lived on Haukøya and travelled widely as a lay preacher. Of the temperance society's banner it says: “It was exceedingly fine too.”
blocks.90: “On a light blue cloth that reached from the ceiling to the floor the temperance emblem was painted. Above the emblem stood: Gula temperance society, and beneath were two oak branches with acorns, tied together with a red ribbon. The branches stretched up the sides of the emblem, and beneath them stood the society's aim: ‘The good of all’”.
blocks.91: I have included so much from this party because I have found so little about this temperance society. It is also worth noting that this report is in what was then called landsmål. It appears that Nynorsk was now gradually gaining more and more ground in the society's paper, and so, one must assume, in written usage elsewhere in the village too.
blocks.92: “The Gula temperance society” must have “folded”. In the paper “Sogn” for 25 October 1935 we find a report of the founding meeting of the “Tingfred” lodge in Eivindvik, and the report says nothing about “the Gula temperance society”. The founding meeting was held on Sunday 20 October 1935 in “the splendid community hall (which the visitors praised highly)”. “The people of Eivindvik were good at turning up; neither dean nor sheriff was missing from the society, and the parish clerk was organist; the meeting hall was completely full.”
blocks.93: “The main hall shone in Good Templar dress, strong and fine colours, thought those who saw it for the first time. Everything was so well prepared.” There were also many visitors, from Bergen and from the neighbouring villages.
blocks.94: “18 new lodge brothers and sisters were initiated. The initiation ceremony (in 3 parts) was unforgettably beautiful.”
blocks.95: Everyone thought the name “Tingfred” (peace of the assembly) was a lovely name that recalled the old assembly site in Gulen.
blocks.96: “These became officers: L.F. (on recommendation) Johs. Norstein, Ø.T. Erling Wevling, V.T. Trygve Lund, S. Agnes Langenes, F.S. Kristine Bøe, Sktm. Lydia Hansen, M. Lydia Wevling, F.B. Anna Norstein, Stl. Alida Larsen, F.Ø.T. O. Vevling, K. Elida Grønevik, D.V. Odd Korsvold, V. Kåre Henriksbø, V.M. Brynhild Underthun, V.S. Hildur Midtun.”
blocks.97: “The new officers were installed, they took their places, and we must say they did well.”
blocks.98: “A great many greetings and good wishes for the new lodge” were presented.
blocks.99: “Faith and enthusiasm carried the good words that were spoken; an unforgettable solemn occasion for each and every one”.
blocks.100: “On the way home several lodge members said they had never experienced such a founding meeting”. This lodge was active after the war of 1940–45 too, but it is now a long time since it was active.
blocks.101: Sunday school gathering in Eivindvik. This is probably from the farewell day for the leader, Solveig Midthun, who left the village in 1927. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.102: The Sunday school was a fixed institution in the village until about 20–30 years ago, and almost all children probably attended it. I have found an old picture from a Sunday school gathering in the 1920s.
blocks.103: I hope someone will take on the study of the various societies and organisations that have existed in the village. The youth society, the rifle club and the sports club, which are all active, will probably celebrate their milestone anniversaries, hopefully with anniversary publications. A great deal of voluntary work has gone into all the societies; the sports ground is perhaps the largest voluntary project in the village, at least in recent times.
blocks.104: Eivindvik school band was started in 1973 as the first school band in Gulen. The school band has been, and is, a great pleasure for the villagers on many occasions, not least every 17th of May. In the relatively few years the band has been active, it has given the village much good culture and created interest in and joy of music, both among the active girls and boys and for those of us who have listened to, and marched to, the music.
blocks.105: In 1969 came “Eivindvik Vel” (the village improvement association), which works for the good of the village in various ways. Among other things it founded “Eivindvik boat club”, which at first was a sub-department of “Eivindvik Vel”. The boat club was founded in 1981, when the first stage of the marina was built, also a great voluntary effort. “Eivindvik Vel” also arranged for the street lights in the village to be put up.
blocks.106: The organisations and societies made the village livelier and the community richer and more pleasant. They gave people a change from their daily toil, and they created more contact with the surrounding hamlets too. “Fremad” mentions that “youth rallies for Gulen” were held. In the summer of 1906 the rally was to be held in Eivindvik.
blocks.108: The ferry boat Lillegutt. Photo: Lent by Bjarne Dåe.
blocks.109: From 6 April 1908 we find a piece about a pleasant trip to a party at the “Elisabetminde” temperance society in Sygnefest. The party had also been up to Vatne, and there was much praise for the programme and the food. The trip was made in the doctor's boat “Lillegutt”. I have heard that this was the first engine-driven ferry boat in Sogn og Fjordane. The boat had a steam engine, and it is said that the boatman, Hans Hermansen (in Prestneset), had to get up very early to stoke up and “get steam up” when the doctor was to go out. Later Jon Henriksbø (in Brekka) skippered this boat. From what I have heard, he was also one of the boatmen for both priest and doctor in the days before engines, when they rowed and sailed on the long journeys. There must have been many exhausting trips in all kinds of weather.
blocks.110: I have tried to find out a little more about this doctor's boat “Lillegutt”. Alf Sæternes and Lars Nygård believe that Dr Nilsen had two boats called “Lillegutt”; the first had a steam engine.
blocks.111: Lars Nygård says the steamboat had a funnel about amidships, had a rather “pointed” bow, and was probably between 30 and 35 feet long. The second “Lillegutt”, Nygård believes, was clinker-built and about the same size as “the steamer”. This new boat first had a “Gideon” engine, later replaced by a “Rapp”, and the boat was fast. At first “Lillegutt” had no wheelhouse. Sæternes says that when Nilsen stopped working as a doctor and moved away (in 1925), the boat was sold to Masfjorden. The last time the boat was in Eivindvik, Sæternes believes, was at the end of June 1935, when it was used as a funeral boat at the burial of Eirik Sæternes. (It was relatives of Eirik who owned the boat.)
blocks.112: With information from an old man at Takle, Mons Takle, Bjarne Dåe (the head of schools) says that the boat earlier sailed in a kind of freight service on the Sognefjord and that, according to Mons and others, there was only one “Lillegutt”. The steam engine was eventually replaced by a motor, but the boat was the same old one. Dåe also says that the first owner of “Lillegutt” in Masfjorden was Arne Brugger, that Hans G. Daae (Bjarne's brother) bought the boat in 1951 and that “Lillegutt” later sank in Nordåsvatnet.
blocks.113: In the inspection of 15 August 1908 the parsonage supervisory board writes that they have no objection to a slipway being put up “for scraping the bottoms of motorboats on the stretch between the bathhouse and the boathouse”, but they oppose “leasing out boathouse sites on the stretch between the municipality's property and the old bathhouse site, since this stretch of shore is considered necessary as a landing place for the churchgoing common people”. The reason for these minutes was probably that Dr Nilsen had applied for such a slipway for his boat, and the minutes of 2 September 1912 show that Nilsen, with the ministry's consent, had put up such a slipway. The board writes: “..and the parish priest shall be granted the right to use this slipway free of charge for scraping the bottom of his motorboat.” I have seen nothing about the parish priest Ottesen having a motorboat. Perhaps they had in mind a possible future motorboat for the parish priest.
blocks.114: The old bathhouse probably stood where Eivindvik Slipp og Mek. verkstad now lies. The parsonage boathouse stood at the landing place west of Astrid Haveland's boathouse.
blocks.115: Sheriff Bredvik also got himself a boat; according to the local history it was the first motorboat in Gulen. It came in 1905 and was called “Veslemøy”.
blocks.116: Sigurd Trædal, who was district doctor here from 1925 to 1939, bought a small aircraft that he used for his official journeys in the municipality. Aircraft were a rare sight here at that time, and it is said that when he came in his plane, people ran out to look at “the wonder”. They forgot they were ill, and got better.
blocks.117: In earlier times many buildings stood at the parsonage that are now gone. We find something about this in the local history, which among other things refers to some documents presented on 26 October 1698 showing that there were then 15 buildings in all, plus “an old, decayed sheep house, quite useless and falling down.”
blocks.118: Borgstova is considered the oldest building now standing in the area; it seems it was part of an old parsonage that stood there. When the parsonage built in 1902 was put up, at the signing of the building contract between the parish priest Ottesen and the master builder Korsvold (in Fonna), dated 28 February 1902, a contract was also made between the same parties for moving and altering “the old priest's house (not the main building) and its interior into a Borgstue and cookhouse at Gulen parsonage.”
blocks.119: As written earlier, cleaning of Borgstova is mentioned in the instructions for the church caretaker of 19 November 1900. So there must have been a Borgstove at Borggarden before the one that came with the rebuilding of the old priest's house in 1902.
blocks.120: Borgstova was used for many things; among other things I know that the sports club's gymnastics group practised there for a while. Now it serves as a tool shed for the municipality. The old root cellar, under the rocky slope north of the church, used to be the storage place for root vegetables at the parsonage.
blocks.121: Joint outings were also arranged within the village; among other things it seems that the many trips, both summer and winter, to the summer-farm huts in Midtundalen were very popular. Once – this must have been on a more casual trip – the party had forgotten to bring matches. They had to have a fire in the stove, and then someone thought of lighting the fire by firing a shotgun. They tried it, but achieved nothing except covering themselves in soot and gunpowder smoke. After two attempts they gave up. “Fremad” has a piece about this. I have also heard people talk about it.
blocks.122: People looked forward to getting together at the meetings and parties, and on the outings. After hard work all week it was good to meet for pleasant company at the weekends. Taking an active part in the work of the societies, and in the various forms of cooperative ventures that gradually came along, also gave people more enthusiasm and interest in the work of farming. There was more life and well-being. In summer there was usually a pause in the work of the societies. There was so much to do outdoors in the light, warm season, and people were so busy with haymaking and other harvesting, that there was not much time left over for the societies.
blocks.124: In spring there was lambing and the spring work, with breaking the soil, ploughing, harrowing, manuring, sowing, planting potatoes and everything needed to get a good crop in the autumn. In spring the farm also had to be cleared, that is, all the hayfields were gone over with a rake, and stones and other bits and pieces were raked together and carried away.
blocks.125: When the warmth had properly come into the air, the sheep were sheared and let out to graze. The day the cows were “let loose”, that is, came out of the cowshed, there was a tremendous to-do, frisky as they always were after a whole winter inside in their stalls. Such bellowing and rumbling, running and butting that it was quite a sight. Jakob Sande has written a fine poem, “Når bølingen slepp ut” (When the herd is let out), which describes this excellently.
blocks.126: For a time the animals were brought in again every evening, but when they had got used to “outdoor life” they were “left out”. The evening the cows were to be left out for the first time, a smudge fire was lit (a fire that made smoke), and it seemed as if the animals then understood that they would not come in again until the autumn. Going out to milk the cows was a heavy job all summer long. It was often the women who “went to the cows”, on top of running the house, with the children and everything, and also helping with the outdoor work at home.
blocks.128: Midtundalen: Ragnhild Midtun in front of the summer-farm hut on farm no. 20, holding no. 1. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.129: In earlier times there was a summer farm in Midtundalen, and earlier still there is said to have been a summer farm on Arefjellet, where the hut foundations used to show. As far back as I remember, nobody here in Eivindvik spent the summer at a summer farm. At Midtun and at the parsonage they used the huts in such a way that, after milking in the evening, they spent the night in the hut and then carried all the milk home with them after the morning milking. Later it became the practice to walk both ways, there and back, both morning and evening. Then they had to get up early in the morning; they set off at 4–5 o'clock. They carried the milk on their backs in tin containers. It could be quite a heavy load, and when the yield was at its greatest, someone was often sent to meet the “cow people” to relieve them by taking over the load.
blocks.130: The women who went to the cows took their knitting with them, and on the way, under the heavy load of milk, many fine, warm, good mittens and socks were made, while the “clog post” (the gossip) also “went” lively. For a time in summer the cows were up in the mountains. The juicy mountain grass gave fine, light yellow and extra good butter.
blocks.131: In spring, before the cows were let out, there was a joint effort to put the boundary walls in order, also up in the mountains. The holdings on each farm were jointly responsible for maintaining the wall.
blocks.132: Besides at Svartevatnet, where the hut now stands, I have heard that the parsonage used to have summer farms at “Sela” north of Svetjønna, in Navdalsbotn and in Botnane south-east of Mjånes. In even earlier times the priests are also said to have had a summer farm in the outfields above Grøskaret at Henriksbø.
blocks.134: Hay hauling at Midtun in the 1950s. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.135: In summer the seasonal work was at its hardest. In our parents' time they mowed only with the scythe, long-handled and short-handled. When I grew up most people also had a horse-drawn mowing machine. According to the local history, the first mowing machine here was bought by Otto J. Midttun at Henriksbø. That was as early as 1898, and it is said to have been the first mowing machine in Gulen; it was a Deering Ideal. In 1903 a mowing machine came to Midtun as well, to Otto L. Midthun; it was an American Adriance. This machine was in use at Midtun until 1950, when it was sold to Halvor Vatne in Sygnefest, where it was in use for several more years.
blocks.136: One would think there must also have been a mowing machine at the parsonage fairly early, but I have found nothing about this. The old people said of the parsonage that it was so sheltered from the wind there that it was hard to get the hay dry.
blocks.137: In older times the means of transport were horse and sledge, both winter and summer, but later the wheel came more into use and they got wagons and carts. The carts, whose box could usually be tipped up to empty the load, were well suited to spreading manure and carrying smaller things. For hay, “hay wagons” with racks were used. The hay wagons usually had 4 wheels, with steering at the front; the carts only two.
blocks.138: Between the seasonal tasks, haymaking and harvesting, the time was used for work in the forest, felling and preparing firewood that was to be hauled home on the snow in winter. In the forest the wood was usually cut into lengths suited to laying on the sledge, often so that each log was 4 billet lengths. A billet length was 60 cm. The tools in the forest were axe and bow saw. For felling larger trees, big two-man saws (the big saw) with coarse teeth and a handle at each end to pull were used. Often there were two men on the bow saw too, one at each end of the bow.
blocks.139: Here it was mainly birch that was used for firewood. It was good wood, and it gave a lovely smell in the living room when we burned dry birch.
blocks.140: When the trees were felled high up on the slopes, there could be a great deal of toil getting the logs down to where we could reach them with a horse and drag or sled. If there was hard frost without snow, the work could go easily; the logs slid long distances on the frozen, slippery ground. In some places we used a cableway. That usually went well. If there was a little drizzle or rain, the wire was in a way lubricated by the wet, and the bundles of wood went whizzing down. Then we sometimes cut the logs into two-ell lengths, sawed them almost through in the middle, bent them together, hung them over the wire and sent them off. That went fine too.
blocks.141: At home on the farms, usually early in spring, the wood was cut into billet lengths, split and stacked to dry. The splitting was done with axe and wedges and was hard work. Splitting 3 cubic measures of wood was a normal good day's work for a man. The cutting was done with a bow saw until electrically driven circular saws came into common use here after the war.
blocks.142: Some also cut peat for fuel. I remember that the people at Stien had a peat hut behind Grytehogen.
blocks.143: In the time between haymaking and the autumn harvest, they also lopped, prepared and dried bundles of leafy branches, which in winter were used as supplementary feed for the animals, especially the sheep. There were no more goats here when I grew up. Another supplementary feed was heather, some of which was cut and used in spring before the animals were let out.
blocks.144: In older times it was usual for the farmers, when the haymaking at home was finished, to mow hay in the outfields. The holdings each had their own strips that they harvested. The hay was “transported” down the slopes in bundles (large sacks of net which, stuffed full of hay, were rolled down the slopes), dried and stored in small stone barns, and hauled home on the winter snow. Those who took part in this outfield mowing usually lived in the summer-farm huts, and I have heard that the farmhands around the farms looked forward to this “outfield mowing time”.
blocks.145: Before the world war of 1940–45, silage was rare. Almost all the hay and aftermath was dried, but some aftermath was stacked. The grain was cut with a sickle, or mown with a scythe, and later with a mowing machine, tied into sheaves and dried on poles or racks. I do not remember the old way of threshing with a flail, but the older people talked about it. It was hard work to stand day after day threshing with the flail. The flail was replaced by the threshing machine.
blocks.147: Threshing needed a lot of help, and neighbours cooperated on it. Usually the threshing machine was driven by hand, by two men standing at the cranks on either side of the machine. “Turning” the threshing machine was heavy, and the men took turns at the cranks. Some used a turbine and water power. During the war (1940–45) Lars Oppedal (he lived in what we called “Mottevika”) went around the farms helping people with threshing with a small oil engine that drove the threshing machine.
blocks.148: After threshing there were several days of winnowing, when the grain went through the winnowing machine to clean it of chaff and other bits. Compared with the threshing machine the winnowing machine was easy to turn; one man managed it fine on his own. It had several sieves, coarse at the top, finer further down and the finest at the bottom. The sieves moved back and forth, and under the machine the clean grain was collected in a trough and emptied into sacks. Inside the machine was a fan that blew the light chaff away. Sometimes even the “clean” grain had small bits of straw in it, so a child was often posted by the trough to pick out any bits. Earlier, before the winnowing machine came, the grain was winnowed in a trough. The trough was shaken up and down so that the chaff blew out and the grain itself was left in the trough.
blocks.149: After winnowing, the grain was stored in bins with lids, free of rats and mice, and dry. Around the farms there were mill houses along the streams. I remember two such along Kvernhuselva at Midtun, but there had been three. One, the one belonging to Ytre Midtun, still stands. All the writing scratched into the walls there recalls many a long night at the mill.
blocks.150: Before milling, the grain was dried well on drying slabs, large iron slabs lying on stone-built ovens. A wood fire was lit under the slabs, and during drying the grain had to be stirred constantly so that it did not burn. At the mill the dried grain was emptied into a wooden hopper. The hopper stood over, and narrowed down towards, the upper millstone, and ended in a kind of funnel, where the opening was regulated by a board with a peg as a stop. On the outside of the hopper the “shaker stone” ran through two blocks with holes in them down onto the millstone. When the water wheel turned the stone, this shook so that the grain slid through the “funnel”, down into the eye of the stone, in between the millstones, and came out again as flour in the bin in front. Freshly ground flour was warm and both smelled and tasted “very” good. The water power was strongest at night. Then the millstone turned faster, the shaker stone shook more and the opening of the hopper had to be adjusted. During the war (40–45) the village mills were sealed by the Germans.
blocks.152: Not long after the war (1940–45) grain growing came to an end in our parts. The kinds of grain most grown here were oats and barley. To get the better of the weeds, various sprays were gradually used, and during the war weed sprayers (backpack sprayers) came into use. These sprayers were also used in the fight against potato blight.
blocks.153: At harvest it was usual for the potatoes to be dug or ploughed up, picked by hand, emptied into boxes and hauled home for frost-free storage, usually in the cellar. The only person I can remember who had a potato lifter, drawn by a horse, was Ivar Henriksbø.
blocks.154: I will mention here that Gerhard Wergeland once took out a patent on a fork specially suited to lifting potatoes.
blocks.155: Horse-drawn manure and fertiliser spreaders were in use here. Ivar Henriksbø also had a hay tedder and a horse rake. Ole J. Midtun also had a horse rake. Horse-drawn drag rakes were also used; I remember that we had one at home. As the farmers went over to silage, the old ways of drying the hay, spreading and drying on racks, were used less and less, and the usual haymaking tools gradually went out of use. The drag rake was probably the one that stayed in use longest.
blocks.156: When spreading, the hay was spread out over the field, turned around midday and gathered (raked together into heaps or windrows) in the evening. The same processes were repeated every day until the hay was dry enough to be taken into the barn. It took two to three days, depending on how thick the grass and how suitable the weather was. When drying on racks, the hay usually stood on the rack for up to a week, often longer if the weather was bad.
blocks.157: In time the tractors came, with trailers and other implements such as harrows, rotary tillers, ploughs, manure and fertiliser spreaders, mowers, potato lifters, log splitters and the forage harvester, which is now the usual harvesting machine for hay. The first tractor to come to the village was the two-wheeled tractor of Sigurd Haveland, who rented the parsonage farm. It was an 8 hp “Hummel” with a mower blade. The first four-wheeler was bought by Rolf Midtun. It was a 17 hp “Farmall”. The two-wheeler came in 1953, the “Farmall” in 1957. Now there are tractors and motor mowers on every holding.
blocks.158: In winter the vehicles were horse and sledge, or sleigh if only people or lighter loads were to be carried. There were several kinds of sledge: box sledges used for carrying manure, for example; stone sledges, which were low so that heavy stones could be got onto them more easily; and wood sledges for hauling firewood from the forest and other ordinary transport. To drag logs into place in rough forest terrain, a drag or sled was used.
blocks.159: When driving a sledge, at least when using the sleigh, a bell was used on the horse.
blocks.161: All the holdings here had shore rights and boathouses. At Midtun they had their boathouses at Stien, at Henriksbø on lower Henriksbø and at Undertun. I have heard that in older times the farms in Midtunvågen also had seine-net fisheries. The last seine fishery in operation here was run by Nils Navdal (at Haugane) and Ola Flolid. They fished with a small beach seine until some years after the war (40–45).
blocks.162: The forest was used in many ways, mostly for fuel, but suitable logs were taken to the sawmill and cut into boards and planks. The sawing was mostly done at Dingja or at Eidssaga.
blocks.163: From suitable timber, blanks were picked out for various things, for example sledge runners, sledge stakes, rake teeth, scythe handles, tool handles and much more. Birch bark was used for roofing and bark for tanning; tough, supple twigs were used for withies and bindings of various kinds; the leaves were, as mentioned, used for fodder, and so partly were the thinnest twigs, which the animals liked to gnaw on. Brooms were also made of twigs, especially birch twigs; scouring brushes for pots were made of scrubbing twigs; from juniper they boiled a juniper lye that was used for cleaning and also for brewing beer. Juniper was also used for basket-making and for making creels, boxes and other containers; rowan bark was sometimes used for fodder, and the innermost part of the bark was even good for people to chew. Rowan was very supple and could be used for things that had to be bent, for example cow collars. Rowan and willow were good for making whistles because the bark came off easily early in spring. Skis were also made of rowan; they were nimble and we thought they ran especially well. Rowan must not be used on board boats, some said; according to old superstition it was dangerous. There was something they called “flograun” (rowan growing on another tree).
blocks.164: This was a short list of some of the things the forest was used for, but the list could have been much longer.
blocks.165: Some used bearberry heather for firewood; it, and what we called small wood (twigs and thin branches), burned quickly and gave strong heat, and was fine for boiling coffee, for example, which almost always had to be done quickly. The bearberry heather was pulled up; other heather was cut with a sickle.
blocks.166: People sometimes picked and dried moss, which was used as bedding in the animals' pens. The moss then mixed with the dung and made good manure. In older times moss was used for caulking when building log houses. There was also a kind of moss that was used for dyeing cloth.
blocks.167: When tanning with bark, the bark was chopped into small pieces and put in water in large wooden vats (tanning vats) to draw out the tannic acid. Additives were also used, lime among others I think, but I do not know how the process went. What was to be tanned was then laid in the vat. At home we had a tanning vat; it was oval and about 2 ½–3 m long. It was not in use as far as I remember.
blocks.169: The parsonage farm was long the largest farm in the village. This is what it looked like in the 1930s. Photo: Unknown.
blocks.170: During the war (40–45) we used potato haulm and straw for fodder. It was mixed and sent through a machine with a large knife blade, a chopping machine, which we turned by hand and so chopped the mixture of haulm and straw into small pieces. This was then soaked in water, mixed with meal and given to the cows almost as a mash. At the bottom of the haystack a lot of hay seed often collected. This was sometimes gathered up and given to the animals with meal on it. During the war we also got something called molasses, a kind of syrup, which was also used as supplementary feed.
blocks.171: On several farms they had root choppers for cutting turnips and other root vegetables for the animals. Of other tools we used for animal fodder, I remember the hay knife. The dry hay was laid in large heaps in the barn, haystacks, where the hay gradually became so tightly packed that it could be hard to get it loose again for feeding in winter. That was when we used the hay knife to cut the hay into blocks, which were loosened and given to the animals. There was a hay knife in every barn. So there was also a hay hook, used to tear loose hay from the stack.
blocks.172: The work in the cowshed was usually shared between woman and man. The usual livestock were cows, sheep, a pig and a few hens (enough for the household to have eggs for its own use), earlier also goats. Most holdings also had a horse, used as a draught animal. In addition almost everyone had a dog and a cat.
blocks.173: All milking was done by hand. Milking machines did not come to the village until after the war. The first milking machine here (milking into a pail) was got by Harald Nese. That was in 1955. The first milking installation (pipeline system) in Gulen was installed at Rolf Midtun's around 1970.
blocks.174: When a new outbuilding was built at Stien in the early 1930s, automatic drinking bowls for the animals were put in. From what I have been told, these were the first of their kind in the village. Such fittings did not become common in the cowsheds here until after the Second World War.
blocks.175: Slaughtering took place mostly in autumn, and then before Christmas. Here too the resources were well used. Everything was kept and used: skin, meat, offal and blood. Even the intestines were cleaned and used, among other things as casings for sausages. Every farm had a meat grinder, and the offal was ground for sausages among other things. Pressed pork and much other good food were also made, and stored in various ways. The meat was usually salted and dried. They also preserved meat in “Norgesglas” (preserving jars). The preserving itself was laborious, but it was soon made up for when one wanted an easy, good Sunday dinner.
blocks.176: Much of the meat was sold to bring in income, some of it sent to Vestlandske Salslag (the western Norway meat cooperative). These consignments went in so-called “slaughter boxes”, in which the meat was packed wrapped in strong paper. Later they changed to sending the animals for slaughter alive to the cooperative.
blocks.177: The wool was cleaned, carded and spun into yarn, which was knitted into mittens, socks and many other warm, good garments. Some also had looms on which they wove both rugs and cloth.
blocks.178: Spinning, knitting, weaving, embroidery, sewing, patching, mending, cooking, housekeeping and washing clothes were looked after by the women. Embroidery was done, then as now, with needle and thread. So was much of the sewing, but every house had a sewing machine turned by hand. Some had treadle sewing machines. Some houses had a knitting machine. With such machines it was quick to knit jumpers, socks, slippers and whatever else was needed. Those who were good at sewing and knitting, and had time to knit and sew for others than their own household, could often earn a nice bit extra from such work.
blocks.179: Clothes to be boiled were boiled in huge pots, or copper cauldrons, on large stoves (wash stoves) in the wash cellar or cookhouse. In older times, instead of stoves, there were open hearths where a fire was lit under pots, or cauldrons, hanging from large pot hangers. A pot hanger was made of two flat iron bars. One was wide with a large hook at one end, closely notched along the edge and with a loop on the side at the other end. The other bar, somewhat narrower, which slid through the loop on the notched bar, had at its upper end a ring that could move about a pin and fitted into the notches. This sliding bar ended at the bottom in a smaller hook. At the top of the hearth a solid beam ran across, through the masonry walls on both sides, and the pot hanger hung from this beam by its largest hook. From the hook on the sliding bar hung the pot, which could then be moved up and down the notches of the hanger, away from or towards the fire, depending on how much heat was needed.
blocks.180: A “brannfot”, a kind of wash stove, was also used. This was an iron ring standing on three or four feet (of iron or stone), on which they set the pot and lit a fire beneath. The brannfot could be used both in the hearth and outdoors, for example by the river when washing clothes in the summer half of the year.
blocks.181: For washing clothes they had large tubs and washboards. The washboard, a wooden board with small feet and a ribbed steel plate on it, was set in the tub with suitably warm water, and then they rubbed the clothes up and down along the ribbed steel plate. At the top of the washboard there was room for the bar of soap. The soap was usually home-made, boiled on the farm; the raw material was fat.
blocks.182: After washing, the clothes were rinsed thoroughly, often in a river or stream, and many women had chilblains and frozen hands in winter. The clothes were dried on lines, outdoors if the weather was suitable, otherwise indoors, in drying lofts or outbuildings, but also in the warmth of the living room if a garment was needed dry in a hurry.
blocks.183: The housewives took care to do fine work, and clothes, especially everyday wear (shirts, blouses etc.), smaller cloths (especially embroidered ones), embroidered pillowcases, handkerchiefs etc. were finely ironed; outer garments were steamed. For steaming and ironing they used large hollow irons with lids, where the source of heat was glowing coals put inside the iron. There were also smaller, solid cast irons that were heated in iron dishes on the stove.
blocks.184: Larger cloths, duvet covers, plain pillowcases and similar items were “mangled”. In older times mangling was done with a roller and a mangle board. The cloth was laid over a smooth, fine roller, and with the mangle board, a polished board with a handle, they beat the cloth, which with this treatment became smooth and fine. As I remember it, the mangling was done with what we called a mangle, or clothes roller. This was two wooden rollers one above the other in a kind of iron frame. At one end there was a large wheel with a handle. This worked as a crank, and by means of small cogwheels the hand power was transferred to the rollers. With a screw with a wheel on it, at the top of the mangle, one could press the rollers together according to how much pressure one wanted on the cloth. The cloth to be mangled was folded neatly, often dampened a little with water, and fed between the rollers as they were cranked round. On the other side of the rollers the cloth came out even and smooth.
blocks.185: Before the war many houses had no running water. They carried it in buckets from wells and streams. In winter water could often become a problem when the frost lasted a long time. Not so seldom we had to haul water, in barrels, cauldrons or other large containers, from the big river. No small amount was needed for the people and animals on the farm.
blocks.186: Bathrooms were not so common in private houses then, but some had them. At home we had a bathing system where we heated water in a large closed copper cauldron shaped like a cylinder, a kind of wood-fired water heater, where the stovepipe ran lengthwise through the cauldron so that the heat of the smoke from the stove below was also used. The water went straight from the tap into the cauldron, which had both a shower and a tap for a bathtub fitted. This system worked quite well.
blocks.187: The public baths in the community hall opened in the autumn of 1941 as the first public baths in Ytre Sogn. Eivindvik youth society was one of the first youth societies in the country to run public baths. I have also heard that our community hall was the first in the country designed with space for public baths.
blocks.188: For the stove (and the brannfot) in the wash cellar or cookhouse there was also a griddle that was laid over the stove or brannfot and used for baking flatbread, lefse, griddle cakes and other cakes. The dough was kneaded and rolled out on the kitchen table, with a wooden rolling pin, into suitable rounds that were folded and carried to the griddle. There the rounds were rolled out over the griddle with a flat wooden stick (a baking stick). To succeed with the baking one needed even and suitably strong heat, and for that one needed good wood. The finished rounds were stacked and stored in the loft or storehouse. On the evenings when the baking went on, the children, and the adults too, were usually gathered round the griddle. It was fun to break pieces off the crisp, freshly baked rounds of flatbread, and they tasted so good.
blocks.189: Baking of bread, other yeast baking and cakes was done in the kitchen. There the baking was done in the oven of the kitchen range. Here too fine wood and suitable heat were decisive for a good result. The housewives had an incredible knack for getting it right, and good it was.
blocks.190: All kneading was done by hand. So was the whisking, with ordinary whisks or rotary whisks. There was a lot of baking around the farms. People baked their own bread, and there were always kringles and biscuits in the pantry, and often sweet bread too. In my childhood it was usual for children to have birthday parties with lots of cakes and cocoa, and there was often a little “extra” when the adults had birthdays too.
blocks.191: People bought coffee as beans (unground). Every house had a small coffee grinder. They were turned with a crank, and most people my age surely remember well the pleasant sound of the coffee grinder and the good smell of freshly made coffee standing in the pot over the rings of the range, or keeping warm on the stove in the living room.
blocks.192: There is a riddle connected with grinding coffee. It was usually the women who made the coffee, and when they sat grinding, the grinder was often held between their thighs. The riddle goes: “It rumbled and rattled in Grandmother's old thing, below the waist, above the knee – what is it?”.
blocks.193: Tall cast-iron stoves were very common for heating houses. In winter, when there was a lot of burning, in the kitchen, the living room and other rooms, it not so seldom happened that the chimneys got so full of soot that there was a chimney fire.
blocks.194: It was many years after the war (1940–45) before the modern electric machines became common in households here, such as the vacuum cleaner, food mixer, coffee maker, washing machine, tumble dryer, refrigerator, freezer, bread slicer, dishwasher, electric sewing machines and all the other technical aids found in homes today.
blocks.195: As mentioned earlier, grain growing ended here in the years after the last world war. In the warm summers during the war, some, in addition to the usual grains such as oats and barley, also tried wheat, with good results. Indeed, even tobacco was grown at that time. There was very little tobacco to be had during the war, so these plants were tended especially well and many grew them successfully. The large leaves were dried and sent to tobacco factories to be processed into smoking tobacco and chewing tobacco. It was a great occasion when the parcels of finished goods came back from the factory. Some prepared the tobacco themselves by carefully following special recipes.
blocks.196: The quality of home-grown tobacco could hardly compare with what came from traditional tobacco regions, and immediately after the war was over, tobacco growing here came to a complete end.
blocks.197: In addition to grain and potatoes, a good deal of vegetables were grown, such as kohlrabi and carrots, and some cabbage of various kinds. Turnips were grown as animal fodder. The most common kinds of berries were redcurrants, blackcurrants and gooseberries. Some berries were sold to juice factories. There were not many fruit trees here, but there were a number of apple, pear and plum trees in the gardens around. Many were also good at planting ornamental trees, shrubs and flowers around their houses.
blocks.198: When I grew up there was hardly any hunting here, only a little black grouse hunting in spring, and then fox hunting to protect the lambs. A bounty was paid on foxes then, and it was allowed to hunt at the den. People sometimes worked for several days at a fox den to get at the cubs.
blocks.199: That red deer were hunted here earlier was shown by the large antlers that hung over the storehouse door at home (farm no. 20, holding no. 1) when I grew up. After no deer had been seen here for a long time, the deer came back to the outfields in the 1950s and 60s. The first deer I know of to be seen in the outfields here in Eivindvik were 3 deer that Rolf Midtun saw on Kjerringfjellet while gathering sheep in 1957. The first culling permits here were held by Ole J. Midtun and Rolf Midtun, farm no. 19, holding no. 2 and farm no. 20, holding no. 1. Together they got a permit for one animal in 1964 or 65. At that time it was not allowed to shoot calves, the season was short, I think only 2 weeks, and they hunted only on Sundays, so there were not many hunting trips. Magnor Midtun also took part in the hunting trips. It was he who “tempted” Ole and Rolf to apply for the permit. No animal was shot, but on the first hunting trip Rolf, at the top of the inner Sølia, had a hind with a calf at quite close range. He spared the hind so that the calf would not be left motherless. In addition to the permit at Midtun, the following year there was also a permit at Henriksbø, where Mons Haveland and Magnor Midtun went on a few hunting trips.
blocks.200: Gradually more permits were applied for, deer hunting areas were arranged, and the first deer here was shot in Holtedalen in 1965 or 66. It was a hind of 84 ½ kg, and it was Edvard Fosse who shot it. The others in the hunting party were Ole J. Midtun, Johannes Hauge, Leif Hauge and Hall Midthun. In 1966 or 67 a permit was also granted in the parsonage and Grønevik outfields. Magnor Midtun held this permit together with Mons Haveland, and a hind was shot, by Mons, on the slope south of Svartevatnet.
blocks.201: Sea trout used to run up the big river (the Midtun river) in summer, and some fish were caught with dip nets and gill nets, fished with traps and even taken by hand when the water in the river was low. The largest trout I have heard of being caught here weighed 6 ½ kg.
blocks.202: I have heard that Kristian Hanssen once stocked fish in Svartevatnet. Ottar Midtun has said he remembers this; he helped catch fry in the river below “Stampehuset” at Midtun. On 17 July 1977, at 5.35 p.m., my children and I released 12 fry (caught in the river at Midtun) into Espeviktjønna. Neither there nor in Svartevatnet can there have been suitable conditions for the fry; there seem to be no fish in either place now.
blocks.203: It is said that both Hanssen and others stocked fish in several of the tarns in the mountains here, but without result. Hanssen is also said to have stocked fry in Prestevatnet above Hausevika, and there is said to be a lot of fine fish there now.
blocks.204: A LITTLE ABOUT HOW CHILDREN LIVED WHEN I WAS GROWING UP
blocks.205: For my own part I can say that we certainly were not bored. I grew up in “the hard thirties” and during the war, but I cannot say that I missed anything; we were not used to anything else. We started school when we had turned seven; the school year began in the autumn. We went to school 3 days a week, the “lower school” on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday, the “upper school” on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. We were in the lower school for 3 years and in the upper school for 4 years.
blocks.206: In the school library we could borrow books of various kinds. The adults borrowed books from the public library, which was in the town hall and was open every preaching Sunday. Many also had a good number of books of their own, novels, travel books and well-known works. There was a Bible and a hymn book in every house.
blocks.207: In addition to books, people read a lot of newspapers. Few had a radio before the war, and during the war the radio sets were confiscated. The most widely read newspapers here, as far as I can remember, were “Sogn og Fjordane”, “Sogningen”, “Bergens Tidende”, “Gula Tidende” and “Dagen”. Some also took “Ukens Nytt”. A paper almost everyone had was “For Fattig og Rik”. A common magazine was “Syn og Segn”. All farmers had, in addition to other newspapers and magazines, “Produsenten” and “Vestlandsk Landbruk”.
blocks.208: Of children's magazines we read “Norsk Barneblad” and “Magne”. The comic books were also popular. The ones I remember best are “Smørbukk”, “Vangsgutane” and the one about Knut Berg and the monk Tala. Of the various weeklies I think “Nynorsk Vekeblad” was the most read here. Games of various kinds were also an important pastime.
blocks.209: The main subjects at school were religious education, church history, Bible history, Norwegian, reading, writing, arithmetic, geography, history, nature study, physics, chemistry, health education, drawing and singing. Many of the songs and hymns we learned in primary school are still fixed in my memory.
blocks.211: At school, in addition to the ordinary teaching, we also spent a good deal of time putting together programmes for parties the teacher arranged for us. These activities always took place in the evenings, and we were often in the community hall then. There was a stage there, and it was easier to rehearse sketches, plays and other items. We had a Christmas party every New Year's Day. This was called the children's party, and we children were responsible for the whole programme. Besides these parties we also often performed at other events, for example the bazaars of the girls' association “Flittig Lise” (Busy Lisa). In this association the girls had meetings every other week through the winter half of the year. They met in the homes around the village, and they made many fine things that were raffled at a bazaar once a year. The proceeds went to various purposes that helped improve conditions at the school, for example the school library, buying an organ and much more. In my school days almost all the events we children had were held in the community hall. We performed with items such as singing, recitation, choral speaking etc., also at the adults' gatherings, for example at bazaars. We thought it was fun to take part in programmes at events; it was a little reward for the effort of all the rehearsing.
blocks.212: Two days a year the schoolchildren usually took part in tree planting. A lot was planted at Midtun, and we were in Undertundalen and in the parsonage outfields. We thought the planting days were a nice change from schoolwork, and it is good now to see that things have grown where we helped to plant.
blocks.213: It was usual to have a school trip in summer. I know that the children had school trips to Bergen, but during the war it was difficult to go so far, so we had to make do with visiting the nearest hamlets.
blocks.215: Outside school, when our homework was done, we took part in the work on the farm. We thought that was as it should be, and it could often be both interesting and fun. In autumn and spring it was often clearing new land. That was done with spade, fork, pick, sledgehammer, crowbar and lever, and sometimes we used a stump puller, also called a stone buck. We helped as much as we could and were glad when we saw the work making progress. The stump puller was a kind of “crane” made of 3 or 4 poles set up as a pyramid, with an axle between 2 of the poles, cogwheels, two cranks and a wire running through a block fastened under the “top of the pyramid”. With this device we could crank up large stumps and stones. The largest stones, and rocky outcrops, were blasted apart with dynamite and levelled. The drilling was done by hand with an ordinary blasting drill and sledgehammer. The youngest in the “team” usually had the job of holding the drill. Sometimes we got a “rap” over the fingers when the sledgehammer did not hit the drill head as it should. When the hole had become so deep that the drill stood by itself, we often used a drill key to spare our knuckles. It was also easier to turn the drill with a drill key. We also had a small type of sledgehammer, called a one-hand hammer, used when a man drilled alone. He then held the drill with one hand and struck (with the one-hand hammer) with the other. It was important that the drills had a proper cutting edge, and Nicolai in Prestneset saw to that. He was a wizard at sharpening drills and was known for his skill from a long career as a drill smith at larger construction works. There were also forges and anvils on many of the farms in those days.
blocks.216: When blasting we used “old women” of bundled juniper as cover. Seeing the charge go off, and how it went, was exciting, almost the high point of the work.
blocks.217: When the adults were in the forest felling and preparing firewood to be hauled home for the winter, we were sometimes given the task of taking food to the workers. We then went so that we arrived around dinner time, and stayed there until everyone went home in the evening. Sending wood down the cableway was great fun.
blocks.218: Something always happened in the outfields too; now and then we saw a fox, a squirrel, a hare or another forest animal, in the river there were fry, and in the forest birds we did not see at home, for example black grouse, great spotted woodpeckers, woodpeckers and often a family of ducks on the lake.
blocks.219: In the evenings we were often in the cowsheds. “Talking to”, patting, grooming and tending the animals was both interesting and educational. We also helped to clean the passages, fill hay in the mangers, carry water to the animals and much more.
blocks.220: For light in the cowshed “bat lanterns” (storm lanterns) were used. These lanterns were round, with an oil burner, lamp glass and a glass globe outside, all set in an iron frame with a handle to hang and carry the lantern by. Above the lamp glass there was a small metal shield so that sparks would not rise and create a fire hazard. Around the lantern there were iron rings to protect it from knocks when we carried it with us. Usually the lantern hung in its fixed place in the cowshed, but when the work required it, it was also carried around the outbuildings. Carrying the lantern to give light while the adults worked was one of the children's jobs.
blocks.221: We were always there when the cows were let out in spring, when the sheep and lambs were let out to the outfields and when the cows were left out with a smudge fire. It was also a great occasion when the sheep were brought home in the autumn. In the afternoon on the gathering day we would often stand in the farmyard looking up towards Åsane, and we thought it fine and exciting when we saw the long line of animals come past Holtesteinen and down over Holtane.
blocks.222: The animals had names, and each of us children had a cow and a sheep we counted as our own. It was always exciting to see whether my sheep had come home from the mountains and whether the lamb had grown big and fine. We sometimes took the animals to shows, and it was a fine thing if we could come home with rosettes tied on them, white for 1st prize, red for 2nd prize and blue for 3rd prize.
blocks.223: We also had a lot of fun with the pets, the cats and the dogs. They were almost like members of the family. Usually they were very affectionate and loved to play. The steady, soothing purring of the cat lying under the stove in the living room I think I will never forget. The dog was clever and good at guarding the house. It always gave warning when strangers approached, and few dared come near if the dog was home alone.
blocks.225: In the winter half of the year the adults often took a short break from work before going to the cowshed in the evening. It was at twilight, when darkness was falling and before the lights were lit indoors. It was a little too dim to do work that needed light, and a little too early to light the lamps. This was called the twilight hour and was a cosy time for the family, with stories and fairy tales, singing, and music if there were instruments in the house.
blocks.226: After the radio came, we would often listen to the children's hour at this time. Every Thursday we listened to “Bergen local”, and we enjoyed “Kallemann and Amandus, Aunt Amalie and Uncle Tobias”, and were a little proud that the man who played all these parts had close relatives in Fonna. His name was Eriksen, and we thought he was terrific. On Saturdays there was a children's hour from Oslo.
blocks.227: Some also had a gramophone, and that was a big thing; the few records were played over and over again. The gramophones were driven by steel springs and had to be wound between each record, and we sometimes got a little tired of all the cranking.
blocks.229: A very popular thing, especially when we got together at weekends, was playing with “mill men” (little water wheels) in the river, or with toy boats. At Midtun the children long had a fine pond inside the farm, where pasture later came and Rolf has now cultivated the land. There we often went on long voyages to both America and Africa. Dams had been built, quays put up and harbours made, and there was much fun and pastime there with lively shipping and great works maintaining both installations and boats.
blocks.230: In summer, when the water was warm enough, we spent a lot of time in the big river swimming and catching trout; indeed we could often spend whole Sundays there and hardly had time to go home to eat. Sometimes we also went with the adults on trips into the mountains to look for the animals. Then we took salt mixed with meal for the sheep, which came running long distances when we called them. They surely knew the smell of the salt mixture we sprinkled on stones and rocks.
blocks.231: We built huts of leaves and conifer branches, and in spring it was also very popular to make a bow, preferably of rowan, and shoot arrows. We made a special kind of arrow that we called “rasar arrows”. To shoot them we used a strong but supple rowan stick. We tied a short cord to the tip of the rowan stick, and at the other end of the cord we made a big knot so that the cord could be laid in a notch on the arrow. We held the stick with one hand, and with the other we pulled the arrow and bent the stick into a large bow. When we then let the arrow go suddenly, it could fly a long way.
blocks.232: Another popular thing was making wind spinners (small windmills). We carved them from wooden boards. The wind spinners were fastened to poles that we put on fence posts or similar places where they could swing freely in the wind. The spinner itself looked like a propeller and was fixed, often with a nail as axle, on the end of a wooden pole that had a kind of vane at the other end, rather like a weathercock. The pole with the spinner then swung around a nail in the pole on the fence post. It was important to get the whole thing properly “balanced”, so that the spinner always faced into the wind. With a good wind the spinners went really fast, and it was pleasant both to watch and to listen as they raced round like little wheels.
blocks.233: We also played games such as rounders, tip-cat, hopscotch, hide-and-seek, something called “my stick”, last pair out, ring games and many more.
blocks.235: Boats with “splintefylgje” (travelling folk), as people said, often came. These travelling people brought quantities of handmade pails, whisks and other everyday things that they went round the farms selling. They also sold many other things, such as clocks, lace and ornaments. Many of the things were probably what is called “trinkets”, but they were nice to look at, and we children were wide-eyed and impressed when they opened their packs.
blocks.236: They were often skilled tinsmiths and often put up new gutters for people. Sometimes they begged for food. There were sometimes fortune-tellers in the group. Not so seldom the old women in the group smoked pipes; we thought that quite a “sight”, since it was then completely unusual here for women to use tobacco at all. We thought it was a little exciting when these people came. The dogs must have had a “feeling” when the group approached, for there was usually a “barking of dogs” that could be heard a long way off. From older times these travellers had the reputation of not being too particular about taking things they came across and needed, so people were perhaps a little relieved when the boats left again. Jakob Sande has a fine poem about these travelling people; it is called “Fantefylgjet” (The travelling folk).
blocks.237: Other travellers, commercial travellers, also came here now and then: book salesmen struggling with big, heavy packs, people selling farm implements, agents for textile factories, insurance agents and others.
blocks.238: Visits from strangers were a little change from everyday life. Lay preachers and travelling secretaries for various organisations also travelled here, as did people who gave political and other lectures. Those we appreciated most of all were the Salvation Army ladies, who drew many people to their meetings. They played and sang so beautifully. And then there was the secretary for the rescue boats; he always brought a film.
blocks.239: Once the film “Gjest Bårdsen” came here. That was a big thing in those days; I think almost the whole village, both children and adults, gathered in the community hall that evening.
blocks.241: In winter we went skiing and skating a lot when the snow and conditions were right. If the snow was wet, with poor skiing conditions, we would build snow houses and forts and have snowball fights. We also went sledging; on the crusted snow especially it went like the wind. But the speed was high on the roads too. When we sledged down the slopes from Midtun we glided nicely all the way out to Stireina. Once we took the sleigh from home and, with it full of children, set off down Skoldingen. Down where it met the bog the sleigh runners went through the crust, the sleigh was turned upside down so that it ended up back to front with the runners in the air, and those of us sitting on it were flung out over the crust. No one was hurt to speak of.
blocks.242: It is the many fine moonlit evenings on the ice, when the lake was frozen, often with a small fire on an islet gleaming in the clear ice, together with the times on the ski slopes, that we probably remember best of all; there was life and shouting there. The joy of sport then was surely just as great, and perhaps more natural and genuine, as it is now in the big sports arenas. I hardly think any of us children who grew up then were ever bored. At any rate it does not feel like that when I look back now.
blocks.243: It could certainly be hard going on a small western Norwegian farm and difficult for the adults to make ends meet. Usually there were many mouths to feed in each family. People had to be careful with what they had and make the best use of what nature provided. They had been brought up to do that; they were used to having little, accepted things as they were, and it is often the brightest memories that live longest.
